title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
keywords: raison d'etre to help those who cannot help themselves
Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry
primary_topics: Chapter 7 covers the twenty-three-year stretch (1963-1986) of Art's life as a private lawyer in the marketplace -- opening his own firm after the Salonga apprenticeship with his mentor's blessing, then expanding into the travel industry (Baron Travel Corporation, 1967), tourism leadership (Philippine Chamber of Tourism executive director), and eventually international heights (chairman of the International Division of the American Society of Travel Agents, ASTA, elected at the 1985 Rome convention as the first and only Filipino, first Asian to hold the post). The chapter's argument is that this period -- driven by 'the deprivations of poverty' as 'an unhealed wound' -- represented Art's pursuit of worldly success as compensation rather than calling.

Three corporate directorships that ended in martial-law catastrophe: Continental Bank, Overseas Insurance Corporation, and Pentagon Mines Inc., all controlled by Art's client Vicente Tan -- closed by General Fabian Ver in 1973-1974, taken over by the government 'with neither due compensation nor due process,' Tan himself detained for years on the false suspicion of being a 'front for Communist China.' The chapter names this as one of CJP's formative encounters with arbitrary state power, a doctrinal source of his later due-process jurisprudence.

The Hong Kong-Texas episode (early 1980s): Mao Zedong's Cultural Revolution catalyzing Hong Kong's industrialization, Hong Kong becoming a 'capitalists' haven' through the 1980s-1990s, Art as counsel to a rising conglomerate amassing $2 million in HK stock shares; then a 10-acre, 182-townhouse Texas property in the South Central US growth corridor purchased with $1.35 million ($800k down + $500k + three mortgages), valued by appraisers at over $5 million. The fall came in pairs: Margaret Thatcher's 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration on the return of Hong Kong to China in 1997 sending the Hang Seng Index down >20% and bankrupting the conglomerate; then the Mexican peso devaluation collapsing Texas real estate, the mostly-Mexican tenants leaving, three months of missed mortgage payments triggering automatic bank foreclosure with no right to repurchase.

Civic resurrection through the Rotary Club of Manila -- joining in 1983 (same year as General Fidel V. Ramos, Chief of the Philippine Constabulary who would become President in 1992 and appoint Art to the Supreme Court in 1995), elected RCM president in 1990 with an induction speech at the Manila Hotel Fiesta Pavilion declaring that the Manila Rotary's 'most important commitment is for the Manila Rotary to be for the poor, the afflicted and the weak.' The chapter frames the Rotary period as the rehearsal-ground of the service ethic that would later define CJP's post-conversion life.

The 1986 EDSA Revolution and the bookend reentry of professional possibility -- when 'the country regained its political and economic freedom in 1986 following the peaceful EDSA Revolution, his law practice picked up and flourished as many of his friends assumed top government posts during the presidency of Corazon C. Aquino.' The chapter ends in this restored country, setting up the next chapter's spiritual conversion.

stances.claim: Art's marketplace years (1963-1986) were not vocational but compensatory -- driven by 'the deprivations of poverty' as 'an unhealed wound,' the explicit goal 'to become prosperous and be able to control the lives of other people.' The chapter reads this period as a long detour, not a culmination.
stances.rhetorical_move: compensation-not-calling diagnosis; explicit naming of motive as wound

stances.claim: Worldly success arrived in unprecedented form (ASTA chairmanship in Rome, $2M HK shares, Texas property at $5M appraisal, Rolls Royce and Patek Philippe, society-pages fodder) and so did its emptiness ('no peace and quiet ... no fulfillment in the overindulgence of his appetite and ego ... alienation from his wife and children'). The chapter argues both ends of the polarity were felt simultaneously and acutely.
stances.rhetorical_move: satiety-emptiness paradox; the having that didn't satisfy

stances.claim: The double catastrophe (Hong Kong + Texas) is presented not as bad luck but as Providence's tool -- the same wound-driven striving had hit a ceiling, and the loss became 'a redirection towards that which he had yet to discover.' The chapter's pivot from possessions to mission is presented as inseparable from financial ruin.
stances.rhetorical_move: providential-ruin framing; the fall as the necessary clearing

stances.claim: The Ver closures of Continental Bank, Overseas Insurance, and Pentagon Mines without due process -- and Vicente Tan's multi-year detention as a 'front for Communist China' he was not -- registered with Art as direct experience of arbitrary state power. The chapter implies (without quite naming it) that this is a doctrinal source of CJP's later due-process jurisprudence as Chief Justice.

The Rotary years were rehearsal -- the *raison d'etre* speech of 1990 ('the Manila Rotary be for the poor, the afflicted and the weak'), the explicit Matthew 25:40 quotation, the redirection of 'major treasures, time and talent' toward 'less fortunate brothers' -- anticipated by years the post-conversion service ethic. The civic crystallized what the spiritual would later complete.
stances.rhetorical_move: rehearsal framing; civic prefiguring of religious

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 covers the twenty-three-year stretch (1963-1986) of Art's life as a private lawyer in the marketplace. After three years apprenticing with Salonga, he opened his own firm with the dean's blessing, taught law at two schools (Sampaloc university-belt and an exclusive convent), and pursued worldly success driven by what the chapter names as 'the deprivations of poverty' as 'an unhealed wound': the explicit goal 'to become prosperous and be able to control the lives of other people,' to ensure his five children would never know the deprivations he had. In 1967 he founded Baron Travel Corporation with 5,000 pesos of his own participation, 100,000 from friends, and 20,000 from his father-in-law Joe Carpio -- total ₱105,000 capital that he kept by buying back every benefactor's shares at book value 'but never less than par.' The travel agency, after a money-losing start, became successful, drawing Art into the Philippine tourism leadership network: Benigno Toda Jr. (PAL), Alfredo Montelibano (Sheraton), Antonio Delgado (Hilton), Enrique Zobel (InterContinental), John Gokongwei (the Padre Faura/Pedro Gil land that became Robinsons Place Manila). The international summit came at the 1985 Rome convention of the American Society of Travel Agents (ASTA -- 20,000 members, 128 countries), where on November 15 he was elected chairman of the International Division, the first and only Filipino, the first Asian to hold the post: 'I'd like to believe that my election is really a triumph of the American dream where everyone, even the lowliest in society, can aspire for and be given the opportunity to lead, to serve and to succeed.' Parallel directorships of Vicente Tan's three companies -- Continental Bank, Overseas Insurance Corporation, Pentagon Mines Inc. -- ended in martial-law catastrophe when General Fabian Ver closed them in 1973-1974 'with neither due compensation nor due process,' and Tan himself was detained for years on the false suspicion of being a 'front for Communist China,' never recovering his wealth. Art then explored Hong Kong, where Mao's Cultural Revolution had catalyzed an industrialization-into-financial-hub trajectory; as counsel to a rising conglomerate he amassed $2 million in Hang Seng shares ($20M in today's money) and used the dividends to acquire a 10-acre, 182-townhouse Texas property in the South Central US growth corridor for $1.35 million, valued at $5M+. He lived the imagined glory: first-class travel, Rolls Royce limousines, Piaget and Patek Philippe watches gifted by the conglomerate's watch-collecting owner, society-pages photographs, high-society gossip fodder, half the year abroad. But the polarity was felt acutely: 'no peace and quiet ... no fulfillment in the overindulgence of his appetite and ego ... alienation from his wife and children.' The double catastrophe came in pairs: Margaret Thatcher's 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration announcing the 1997 return of Hong Kong to China sent the Hang Seng down >20% and bankrupted the conglomerate (with reported trader suicides); the Mexican peso devaluation collapsed Texas real estate, the mostly-Mexican tenants left, three months of missed mortgage payments triggered automatic bank foreclosure with no right to repurchase. 'He felt dismally poor again.' Leni's preference for the Philippines decided the next move -- Art declined the US-recovery option and returned home, joining the Rotary Club of Manila in 1983 (the same year as Major General Fidel V. Ramos, the Chief of the Philippine Constabulary who would become President in 1992 and appoint Art to the Supreme Court in 1995). The civic resurrection led to RCM presidency in 1990; at the Manila Hotel Fiesta Pavilion induction Art declared 'our most important commitment is for the Manila Rotary to be for the poor, the afflicted and the weak ... the *raison d'etre*, the reason for being, of Manila Rotary - to help those who cannot help themselves' -- quoting Matthew 25:40 explicitly: 'whenever we do these acts of charity and love for the needy, we really do them for God.' Director roles at PCCI and MAP, the 1986 EDSA Revolution restoring his many friends to top government posts under Cory Aquino, and his law practice 'picked up and flourished' -- closing the chapter at the threshold of the spiritual conversion that the next chapter would describe.
